content:
We have mass spec, carbon NMR, and carbon shift ranges. Need to deduce SMILES.

Mass spec: m/z 211.0764 (most intense). Likely molecular ion [M]+? Possibly M+H? Usually ESI positive gives [M+H]+. So molecular weight ~210.07 (if M+H = 211.076). So neutral M = 210.069. Let's compute possible formula.

Carbon NMR peaks: 168.30, 130.70,130.27,128.35,126.66,124.85,123.57,58.70,36.40,36.40,26.40.

Interpretation: 168.3 ppm suggests carbonyl carbon of ester (C=O of ester ~170-175). 58.7 ppm suggests O-CH2 (e.g., ethoxy). 36.4 (two equivalent) maybe CH2 adjacent to carbonyl? 26.4 maybe CH3.

Aromatic carbons: many peaks around 124-131 ppm typical for phenyl ring.

Thus likely aromatic ester with ethyl group: e.g., ethyl benzoate (C9H10O2? Actually ethyl benzoate formula C9? Wait benzoic acid C7H6O2, plus ethyl adds C2H5O => C9H10O2? Let's compute: benzoic acid C7H6O2, ethyl ester C9H10O2? Actually ethyl benzoate is C9H10O2? Let's check: benzoic acid C7H6O2, replace OH with OCH2CH3 adds C2H5O, net C9H10O2? But need carbon count: C7 + C2 = C9, H6-1 (lost H) +5 =10, O2 unchanged? Actually benzoic acid has C7H6O2, ethyl ester C9H10O2. Molecular weight: C9=108, H10=10, O2=32 => 150. Not 210.

Our mass 210 suggests maybe phenyl acetate with extra groups. Let's compute possible formula: C13H14O2? C13=156, H14=14, O2=32 total 202. Not 210.

Maybe C12H14O3? 12*12=144, H14=14, O3=48 total 206. Not.

C13H18O3: 156+18+48=222.

C11H10O4: 132+10+64=206.

C12H14O4: 144+14+64=222.

We have carbonyl at 168 (ester). Also aromatic ring (6 carbons). So total carbons maybe 9-10? Let's count carbon NMR peaks: 11 distinct signals (some duplicates). 1 carbonyl (168), 6 aromatic (130,130,128,126,124,123) that's 6, O-CH2 (58.7), CH2 (36.4 duplicate maybe two equivalent CH2), CH3 (26.4). That's total 1+6+1+2+1 =11 carbons. So molecule likely C11.

Check: C11 with carbonyl (ester) and ethoxy group (CH2CH3) gives O-CH2 (58.7) and CH3 (26.4). The CH2 at 36.4 maybe benzylic CH2 attached to carbonyl? For example phenylacetate (phenylacetic acid ethyl ester) would have CH2 between phenyl and carbonyl. That CH2 would be around 35 ppm. Yes.

So candidate: ethyl phenylacetate (ethyl 2-phenylacetate). SMILES: CCOC(=O)CH2C6H5 => "CCOC(=O)CC1=CC=CC=C1". Let's compute formula: C11H12O2? Wait count: ethyl (C2H5O) + carbonyl carbon (C=O) + CH2 (C1H2) + phenyl (C6H5). Total C = 2+1+1+6 =10? Actually carbonyl carbon is already counted as part of C=O, that's one carbon. So total C = ethyl (2) + carbonyl (1) + CH2 (1) + phenyl (6) =10. Wait that's C10. Let's recount: Ethyl group: CH3-CH2-O- (C2). Carbonyl carbon: C=O (C1). CH2 attached to carbonyl: CH2 (C1). Phenyl ring: C6. Total C = 2+1+1+6 =10. So C10. But we observed 11 carbons. Maybe there is also an extra carbonyl carbon? Actually carbonyl carbon counted already. So maybe molecule is ethyl benzoate (C9? Wait ethyl benzoate has phenyl attached directly to carbonyl, no CH2). That would have carbonyl carbon (1), phenyl (6), ethoxy (2) =9 carbons. Not 11.

Our NMR shows 11 carbons, includes carbonyl, aromatic 6, O-CH2, CH2 (maybe two CH2?), CH3. That's 1+6+1+2+1 =11. So there are two CH2 groups: O-CH2 (ethyl) and CH2 adjacent to carbonyl (benzyl). That matches ethyl phenylacetate (C10). Wait ethyl phenylacetate has O-CH2CH3 (two carbons) and CH2 between carbonyl and phenyl (one carbon). That's total carbons: phenyl 6 + carbonyl 1 + CH2 1 + ethoxy 2 =10. So only one CH2 besides O-CH2. But we have two CH2 signals (both at 36.4 duplicate maybe same environment? Actually duplicate could be two equivalent CH2? But they are same shift, maybe two CH2 groups equivalent? Could be O-CH2 and CH2 both at similar shift? But O-CH2 is at 58.7, distinct. So the duplicate 36.4 could be two CH2 groups equivalent, maybe a -CH2-CH2- chain (propyl). So maybe ethyl 3-phenylpropionate? That would have phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOEt. That gives two CH2 groups (benzylic ~35, next ~30). But both appear same 36.4 maybe overlapping.

If we have phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOEt, carbon count: phenyl 6, CH2 (benzylic) 1, CH2 (next) 1, carbonyl 1, ethoxy 2 =11 carbons. Yes matches 11.

Carbonyl at 168 (ester). O-CH2 at 58.7. Two CH2 at 36.4 (maybe overlapping). CH3 at 26.4 (ethyl methyl). Aromatic 6 peaks.

Thus candidate: ethyl phenylpropionate (ethyl 3-phenylpropanoate). SMILES: CCOC(=O)CCC1=CC=CC=C1? Wait chain: phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOEt. So SMILES: CCOC(=O)CCc1ccccc1? Actually carbonyl attached to CH2CH2-Ph. So carbonyl carbon attached to CH2 (alpha) which attached to CH2 (beta) attached to phenyl. So SMILES: CCOC(=O)CCc1ccccc1. Count: CCO (ethyl) O C(=O) C C c1ccccc1. Carbons: ethyl 2, carbonyl 1, two CH2 2, phenyl 6 =11. Good.

Now check mass: formula C11H12O2? Let's compute: C11 = 132, H? Ethyl: CH3CH2O- gives CH3CH2O (C2H5O). The rest: carbonyl carbon no H, CH2-CH2-Ph gives CH2CH2C6H5 = C8H9? Actually CH2CH2C6H5 = C8H9? Let's count: CH2 (2 H), CH2 (2 H), phenyl C6H5 (5 H). Total H = 2+2+5 =9. Add ethyl H5 =14. So total H =14. O2. So formula C11H14O2. Molecular weight: C11 132, H14 14, O2 32 = 178. Not 210.

Our mass 211 suggests heavier, maybe includes chlorine or bromine? But carbon NMR shows only carbons up to 168, no halogen effect. Could be C12H14O2? That would be 210 (C12=144 +14+32=190). Wait 144+14+32=190. Not 211.

Maybe there is an extra oxygen (e.g., ester + carbonyl + maybe additional O). But mass 211 suggests maybe C12H15O3? 144+15+48=207. Not.

Let's compute exact mass for C11H14O3: 132+14+48=194. Not.

C12H14O4: 144+14+64=222.

C13H14O2: 156+14+32=202.

C13H18O2: 156+18+32=206.

C13H22O2: 156+22+32=210. That's close to 210.07. So maybe formula C13H22O2 (mass 210.16). But carbon NMR shows aromatic carbons, so not saturated.

C13H14O3: 156+14+48=218.

C12H18O3: 144+18+48=210. So C12H18O3 could be 210. But aromatic? Not.

Thus maybe mass includes sodium adduct [M+Na]+ at 211.076, meaning M = 188.07. If [M+Na]+ = 211.076, subtract 22.989 = 188.087. That could be C11H12O3? 132+12+48=192. Not.

Or [M+H]+ = 211.076 => M = 210.069. Could be C13H14O2? 202. Not.

Let's compute exact mass for C13H14O3: C13 156.000, H14 14.109, O3 47.985 = 218.094. Too high.

C12H14O3: 144+14+48=206. Not.

C12H10O4: 144+10+64=218.

C11H10O4: 132+10+64=206.

C10H14O4: 120+14+64=198.

C9H10O5: 108+10+80=198.

Maybe the mass includes chlorine isotopic pattern? The spectrum shows peaks at 211, 212, 213 etc with decreasing intensities, typical of chlorine (Cl isotopes 35/37 ratio 3:1). But pattern: 211 (100), 212 (12), 213 (33) not typical. For chlorine, M+2 about 1/3 intensity. Here 212 intensity 12% of 211, 213 33% of 211. Could be bromine? M+2 similar intensity. Not.

But pattern shows multiple peaks spaced 1 Da, maybe due to isotopic distribution of carbon (13C). Not helpful.

Given limited tools, maybe we can simulate spectra for candidate and compare? But we cannot view experimental proton NMR etc. Only have carbon NMR and mass. Could try to simulate for ethyl phenylpropionate and see if carbon shifts match.

Let's simulate.
